content: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction is one of the most commonly performed orthopedic procedures. A frequent technical reason for failure in these surgeries is the incorrect positioning of the graft. Computer-assisted surgery (CAS) has been developed with the goal of improving the precision of graft placement. Although injuries to the posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) and subsequent reconstructions are less common, they present similar challenges in terms of accurate graft placement. This document is an update of a Cochrane review that was initially published in 2011. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of computer-assisted reconstruction surgery compared to conventional surgical techniques for ACL or PCL injuries in adults. For this update, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Bone, Joint and Muscle Trauma Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL, covering the period from 2010 to July 2013. References from relevant articles and prospective trial registries were also reviewed. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomized controlled trials that compared CAS with conventional surgical techniques for ACL or PCL reconstruction. Two independent reviewers screened the search results, assessed the risk of bias in the included studies, and extracted data. When appropriate, data were pooled using risk ratios (RR) or mean differences (MD), both with 95% confidence intervals (CI). The updated search identified one new study, bringing the total number of included RCTs to five, with a combined total of 366 participants. The majority of participants were female (70%), and their ages ranged from 14 to 53 years. All trials focused on ACL reconstructions performed by experienced surgeons. However, the assessment of bias in these studies was limited by poor reporting of trial methodologies. As a result, several studies were classified as having an unclear risk of bias. One trial, which provided primary outcome data, was judged to have a high risk of detection bias due to the lack of clinician blinding and attrition bias from unaccounted loss to follow-up at two years. Moderate-quality evidence from three trials involving 193 participants indicated no clinically significant difference between CAS and conventional surgery in International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) subjective scores. These scores, which are self-reported measures of knee function, range from 0 to 100, with higher scores indicating better function. Pooled data from two of these trials (120 participants) showed a small, clinically irrelevant difference favoring CAS (MD 2.05, 95% CI -2.16 to 6.25). A third trial (73 participants) also reported minimal differences in IKDC subjective scores (MD 0.2). Low-quality evidence from two trials involving 120 participants showed no difference between CAS and conventional surgery in Lysholm scores, which are also measured on a 0 to 100 scale, with higher scores indicating better function (MD 0.25, 95% CI -3.75 to 4.25). Very low-quality evidence from one trial with 40 participants showed no difference in Tegner scores between the two groups. Additionally, low-quality evidence from three trials involving 173 participants indicated that the majority of participants in both groups were assessed as having normal or nearly normal knee function (86/87 with CAS versus 84/86 with conventional surgery; RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.06). No differences were observed between the two groups in secondary outcomes, including knee stability, loss of range of motion, and tunnel placement. None of the trials reported on the need for re-operation. Two trials involving 133 participants reported no adverse post-surgical events, while the remaining three trials did not report on this outcome. CAS was associated with longer operating times compared to conventional techniques, with the mean difference in operating times ranging from 9 to 27 minutes across the studies. In conclusion, based on the currently available evidence, it is not possible to confirm or refute a beneficial effect of CAS for cruciate ligament reconstruction of the knee compared to conventional surgical techniques. The evidence does not suggest that CAS improves outcomes in knee ligament reconstruction. Future studies on this technology should focus on improving the quality of reporting to provide more definitive conclusions.
